LLMs are picking winners. Here’s how to become one.
[![Square profile picture](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/2051741479433822210/YboW6yWw_normal.png)](http://x.com/posthog)

In the last two years, our traffic from LLMs grew 41x. Every quarter set a new record with no signs of slowing down.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKfE4fXbsAAlS4D?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/posthog/article/2065133771817619628/media/2064835428944162816)
Stonks
If you’re a skeptic like me, you’re probably about to ask: “WeLL, BuT dOeS iT cOnvErT?”
Yes, yes it does. Better than almost anything else we have.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKfE9D2asAAwSlk?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/posthog/article/2065133771817619628/media/2064835507457273856)
More stonks
I’m not telling you this to humble brag (well, maybe a little). I’m telling you because the inverse is also true.
PostHog has
[14 products and counting](https://posthog.com/products?utm%5Fsource=posthog-newsletter&utm%5Fmedium=post&utm%5Fcampaign=aeo)
, and (sadly) not all of them are recommended by LLMs at the same scale or rate. While most models know us for
[product analytics](http://posthog.com/product-analytics?utm%5Fsource=posthog-newsletter&utm%5Fmedium=post&utm%5Fcampaign=aeo)
,
[session replay](https://posthog.com/session-replay?utm%5Fsource=posthog-newsletter&utm%5Fmedium=post&utm%5Fcampaign=aeo)
,
[error tracking](http://posthog.com/error-tracking?utm%5Fsource=posthog-newsletter&utm%5Fmedium=post&utm%5Fcampaign=aeo)
, and
[feature flags](https://posthog.com/feature-flags?utm%5Fsource=posthog-newsletter&utm%5Fmedium=post&utm%5Fcampaign=aeo)
, fewer acknowledge we also offer a
[data warehouse](https://posthog.com/data-stack?utm%5Fsource=posthog-newsletter&utm%5Fmedium=post&utm%5Fcampaign=aeo)
,
[AI observability](https://posthog.com/ai-observability?utm%5Fsource=posthog-newsletter&utm%5Fmedium=post&utm%5Fcampaign=aeo)
,
[logs](https://posthog.com/logs?utm%5Fsource=posthog-newsletter&utm%5Fmedium=post&utm%5Fcampaign=aeo)
, and a lot more.
This is likely the case for your product too. Changing it requires dipping into the mystical new field of answer engine optimization (AEO), which I’ve learned a lot about as the person responsible for it at PostHog over the last year.
#
1\. Do LLMs even know you exist?
Your first step should be finding out if you’re being mentioned at all.
1. Go to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini (make sure memory is off or private mode is on).
2. Run 3-5 basic prompts a real customer would use like “best X tool” or “alternative to Y” or “recommended Z product.” Being more specific is less helpful here.
3. See where you show up, are missing, or are misrepresented.
If you want a more robust opinion, pick one of the dozens of AEO tools that have launched in the last year.
[ ](https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/llms-are-picking-winners-heres-how?utm%5Fsource=post-email-title&publication%5Fid=1318225&post%5Fid=200629973&utm%5Fcampaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=8i8gsr&triedRedirect=true&utm%5Fmedium=email#footnote-1)
A decent tool runs hundreds of prompts for you every day, which gives a clearer picture into your LLM visibility over time and across models.
Don’t overthink this, choose a tool that fits your budget comfortably and matches your usual analysis workflow.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKfFEibbAAAJgzs?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/posthog/article/2065133771817619628/media/2064835635924631552)
The LLMs and your AEO tool will

🔗 How to grow your AEO function (without losing your mind) - PostHog How to grow your AEO function (without losing your mind) - PostHog

How to grow your AEO function (without losing your mind)
Contents
I learned SEO the traditional way: by telling a client I knew how to do it, then immediately Googling “what is SEO.” I must have done something right, because not long after that I was hired to do it full-time.
Seven years later, fate (and LinkedIn) led me back to a familiar spot.
"Can you lead our AEO efforts?"
"Of course I can," I replied, with a similar sense of mild panic.
The difference was that this time, everyone else in the industry was still figuring it out too. The concept of AEO (or AIO, AISEO, GEO... [insert your preferred acronym here]) had only existed for a few months. We were all still furiously Googling under the table.
A year later, I'm reporting back from the AI optimization trenches with some good news: it works. We're watching it happen in our numbers, in real time.
PostHog's LLM-referred traffic has grown 41x in 23 months, 7.4x year-over-year, and every single quarter since Q2 2024 has set a new record, with no signs of slowing down.
If you're a skeptic like me, you're probably about to ask: "WeLL, BuT dOeS iT cOnvErT?"
Yes, yes it does. Better than almost anything else we have.
I'm not telling you this to humble brag (well, maybe a little). I'm telling you because the inverse is also true.
PostHog has [11 products and counting](https://posthog.com/products), and (sadly) not all of them are being recommended by LLMs at the same scale or rate. While most models know and recommend us for [product analytics](https://posthog.com/product-analytics), [session replay](https://posthog.com/session-replay), [error tracking](https://posthog.com/error-tracking) and [feature flags](https://posthog.com/feature-flags), fewer acknowledge we also offer [a data warehouse](https://posthog.com/data-stack), [LLM observability](https://posthog.com/llm-analytics), [logs](https://posthog.com/logs), and a lot more.
This visibility gap has turned into an obvious handicap for our growth in certain verticals, and closing it is something we're actively working on.
You should be, too. Because if you're not in the conversation, you're not in the game.
For most of the last decade, growth has, among other things, been a function of how many strangers Google could send your way. Now an increasing share of it also depends on how often, and how accurately, an LLM mentions your name when asked for a recommendation.
So, how do you get into the conversation? Start with the boring stuff.
1. The basics are still the basics
Here's the least sexy but most obvious piece of advice: most of ["traditional SEO"](https://posthog.com/newsletter/seo-for-startups) still works.
Good structure, clear writing, semantic HTML, internal linking, fast loading pages, canonical tags, answering the damn question instead of burying it under 400 words of "in today's fast-paced digital landscape…". All of it still matters.
The takeaway here isn't "SEO is dead, long live AEO." It's that SEO and AEO are drinking from the same well, the difference is how they drink it.
Now, the unit of consumption is a chunk, not a page. Your content needs to be citable in pieces, not just useful as a whole.
Which means the "AEO checklist" most of the industry has already agreed on (the things I'm going to treat as settled for the purposes of this post) looks something like:
- Make your content scannable. Subheadings, short paragraphs, lists where lists belong.
- Use natural language. Write like a person explaining something to another person.
- Cut the fluff. If a sentence doesn't add information, delete it.
- Answer questions directly. If someone asks "what is X," tell them in the first sentence. Supporting context comes after.
- Structure for retrieval. H2s that are actual questions, definitions that can stand alone, summary tables, clear data, FAQs.
- Be specific. Models favor content with concrete details (real numbers, named tools, specific scenarios) over content that gestures vaguely at the same idea. "Most teams ha

How to connect Gmail and iMessage to build better relationships
I miss my OpenClaw.
I retired “Agent Twilo” in March when Anthropic banned 3rd party access to the Claude Max plan.
And since then I’ve been looking for alternatives — particularly options with easy access from an iPhone.
This week, I started building a Codex-driven solution that works well inside the ChatGPT app. It was inspired by fintech entrepreneur
[@nicolas](https://x.com/@nicolas)
’ post
[My agent stack for automating my personal life.](https://x.com/nicbstme/status/2060583553449250888)
##
Building my customized personal agent
I’m on my phone all the time.
Texting, emailing, sending screenshots and calling friends.
I share YouTube tutorials, make
[mutually beneficial introductions](https://radreads.co/mututally-beneficial-intro/)
and send birthday videos.
Basically, I use my phone to try to be helpful to others (and get them excited about the possibilities of AI).
I have no interest in replacing this sincere approach with an AI-enabled system.
Yet at the same time, I do want to use AI to give me more moments of serendipity and suggest more ways to help others.
So the goal was simple.
How can I surface interesting insights in my work email (for
[Latourai.com](https://www.latourai.com/)
) and inside my iMessages?
Why these two services? Because that’s where 90% of my communications take place. And iMessage has become a much bigger source of my overall communications.
So I set out to build this using OpenAI’s Codex.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkZlXKaIAAy9hv?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/khemaridh/article/2065211366953369879/media/2065210033789607936)
##
What is a headless CRM?
Headless software is all the rage these days.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkZqUSaYAA-0Lz?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/khemaridh/article/2065211366953369879/media/2065210118917218304)
We’ve got headless CRMs, browsers and business intelligence tools. But what does this term actually mean?
It means there’s no user interface. With headless software, you can’t click and use your mouse. Interactions happen exclusively via text (chat, scripts, APIs and agents).
What does that mean in CRM terms? It means that you can use natural language to interact with your underlying contacts. For example, you could say:
* Tell me which clients have signed a purchase agreement but haven’t closed
* I’m going to a conference in Dallas, which high-quality leads should I pursue while I’m there?
These don’t require an interface. It just requires safely connecting my data to the Codex harness.
##
Step 1: Selecting a harness
The first order of business was where this “app” would be hosted and how I would communicate with it.
Some common “harnesses” are Claude Cowork, Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes and Pi.
I chose Codex because its mobile experience has gotten really good. It can reference all your chats and any required files (and is blazingly fast).
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkZtkBasAAr3u3?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/khemaridh/article/2065211366953369879/media/2065210174680510464)
##
Step 2: Connecting iMessage and Google
This was the trickiest step since it involved using two open source “CLIs” to connect to each service.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkZvaLbAAAnHjQ?format=jpg&name=sma

The fastest way to find real AI leverage inside a company has very little to do with testing the latest model or rolling out another tool.
Teams often focus on visible signs of progress. They share prompt libraries, schedule training sessions, connect new applications, and expand access across the organization. The goal is simple.
Increase usage and hope it leads to better results. Yet the more valuable opportunity is usually hidden in the work itself. It appears in the small moments when people repeatedly improve AI outputs using their own judgment and experience.
I’d start with a five-minute exercise.
Ask everyone on the team one question.
What is one AI correction you made more than once this week?
That question cuts through the noise because it starts with real work. It skips the abstract AI conversation and goes straight to the moments where the model got close, someone with context stepped in, and the output became useful.
Those moments are where the first useful AI skills usually hide.
I’m walking through how to turn these repeated corrections into skills this Friday with Claude and ChatGPT. You can
[join the free live session here](https://hiten.com/how-to-build-skills)
.
##
Repeated Correction Is The Signal
Every team using AI has a version of this problem.
A model drafts a customer summary that includes the facts while missing the risk. Sales prep comes back with account history while ignoring the objection from the last call. A research recap lists the feedback without finding the pattern. A page sounds polished, although the claim still has no proof.
Someone fixes the output and the work gets better. A few days later, the same kind of task shows up and the same correction happens again.
That repeated correction is easy to dismiss as cleanup because the work already moved forward. The useful part is what the correction reveals.
Someone on the team has a method the model does not have yet.
##
The Method Is The Asset
A useful AI skill usually starts with a small frustration.
You keep telling AI to separate facts from inference. Someone else keeps asking it to make the claim more specific. Another person keeps adding customer proof before copy gets polished. A manager keeps rewriting updates so they explain what matters instead of listing what happened.
These corrections look tactical from the outside. Inside the company, they carry judgment.
A strong salesperson can spot the real obstacle in a deal. An experienced support lead can tell when a conversation is heading toward escalation. A sharp marketer recognizes when a claim sounds compelling but lacks proof, while a product person can distinguish isolated feedback from a meaningful pattern.
Companies already have these methods. They live in people’s heads, review comments, Slack threads, old docs, customer calls, and repeated conversations.
AI makes them easier to see because the model keeps almost doing the work.
Almost is the important word. When AI gets close and someone still has to fix it, the fix is worth studying.
##
The Exercise
The exercise should feel simple enough to do during a team meeting.
Ask three to five people what AI output they corrected more than once this week, then listen for the pattern underneath the answers.

is deepset's open-source framework for building production LLM applications: pipelines, agents, RAG, the whole stack. The Agent component handles tool use and conversation control well, but it's stateless across runs. The next session starts cold.
This post is a walkthrough of hindsight-haystack, the integration that adds three drop-in Haystack Tool instances (retain, recall, reflect) and an optional HindsightMemoryWrapper toolset that does the memory work automatically without the agent having to decide when to call a tool.
##
TL;DR
* pip install hindsight-haystack. Two entry points cover both styles of integration:create\_hindsight\_tools() returns a list\[Tool\] you pass to any Haystack Agent. The agent decides when to call them.HindsightMemoryWrapper is a Toolset subclass with auto\_recall and auto\_retain flags. Use
[toolset.run](http://toolset.run/)
(agent, ...) and the memory work runs automatically before and after each turn.
* The same three memory primitives in both: retain stores content, recall searches, reflect synthesizes.
* Drop tools individually with include\_retain / include\_recall / include\_reflect.
* Hindsight Cloud is the recommended path; self-hosted works the same way once you point the client URL at your instance.
##
Why Persistent Memory Matters for Haystack Agents
Haystack's Agent component is fine for a single conversation: it carries the message history through the run and the chat model has it in context. What it can't do is remember anything once that run ends. The next call starts with whatever you pass in messages, nothing else.
For a one-shot RAG endpoint that's fine. For a customer-facing assistant that should remember preferences across sessions, a support agent that should accumulate fixes to known issues, or a research agent that should build up a project model over weeks, you need a layer that survives the run. That's the gap this integration fills.
##
Two Integration Modes
The integration ships two entry points, and they cover the two ways teams typically want to wire memory in.
Mode 1: Tools the Agent Decides To Call
create\_hindsight\_tools() returns a list of Haystack Tool instances. You pass them to Agent(tools=...), and the model decides when to call them based on the tool descriptions and the user's request.
python
```python
from hindsight_client import Hindsight
from hindsight_haystack import create_hindsight_tools
from haystack.components.agents import Agent
from haystack.components.generators.chat import OpenAIChatGenerator
from haystack.dataclasses import ChatMessage
client = Hindsight(base_url="http://localhost:8888")
tools = create_hindsight_tools(
client=client,
bank_id="user-123",
mission="Track user preferences",
)
agent = Agent(
chat_generator=OpenAIChatGenerator(model="gpt-4o-mini"),
tools=tools,
system_prompt=(
"You are a helpful assistant with long-term memory. "
"Use retain_memory to store important facts. "
"Use recall_memory to search memory before answering."
),
)
result = agent.run(messages=[ChatMessage.from_user("Remember that I prefer dark mode")])
print(result["messages"][-1].text)
```
You get three tools by default: retain\_memory, recall\_memory, reflect\_memory. The system prompt tells

Fable follows short, principle-level instructions so reliably that the elaborate scaffolding I'd built to keep earlier models on track — checklists, compliance scripts, sync layers — became dead weight almost overnight. But one problem got more acute with stronger autonomy, not less: sessions still forget.
Every Claude Code session ends mortal. Clear the context, hit auto-compaction, close the laptop, switch machines — and everything the session knew about your project's goals, decisions, and loose ends is gone. So today I'm releasing claude-workstream-kit, a small open-source system that gives any Claude Code project durable, git-versioned work tracking, designed Fable-first. It's what survived when I rebuilt a much larger private system for the new model — and the throwing away turned out to be the interesting part.
##
The reconstruction tax
AI coding sessions are ephemeral by design. The work isn't. A feature lands across a week of sessions. A migration takes a dozen. A research question evolves for a month.
When the work's state lives only in conversation history, every new session pays what I've come to call the reconstruction tax: re-explaining the goal, re-discovering what was decided and why. The visible cost is time and tokens. The quieter cost is drift — a decision made carefully in session three gets remade differently in session nine, because nothing recorded the original reasoning.
Everyone who uses these tools seriously has felt this. The common workarounds each cover a slice:
* A growing CLAUDE.md survives sessions — but it's loaded into every future session forever, and nothing in it ever closes. It becomes a junk drawer.
* The harness's built-in task tracking and plan mode are good within a session, but their state isn't in your repository and doesn't travel.
* Agent memory is for lessons and preferences — account-side, per-fact. It's not a ledger of a project's work.
* GitHub Issues and PRs are the right answer for teams — but their state lives service-side, needs network and auth, and fits code delivery, not exploration.
* A SPEC.md in the repo survives and travels — but has no resume pointer, no record of decided-versus-open, no definition of done.
What none of these provide: work state that is project-scoped, git-versioned, and portable — surviving everything the harness can do, and traveling with the repo like tests or docs.
##
Workstreams: two files in git
The kit's answer is deliberately small. A workstream is a unit of multi-session work tracked in two markdown files committed to your repo:
* workstream.md — everything durable about one piece of work: purpose, a checkbox backlog, decisions with their reasoning, lessons learned, and — this part matters — falsifiable deletion criteria written at creation: the conditions under which this work is done and can be archived.
* ACTIVE.md — a per-project pointer: what's active, the current task, the single next action, what's blocked.
Git does the heavy lifting. Clone the repo and the entire work state moves with it. The commit history is the progress journal. And because the files are flat frontmatter plus checkboxes, a shell one-liner — or a cheap small model — can read project status without any parsing machinery. That last property is what makes delegation and au

Think about a character you have spent 100 hours playing in Skyrim or Elden Ring.
What exactly is your character?
* Is it the game engine? No.
* Is it the PlayStation? No.
* Is it the controller? No.
Your character is the save file.
If your PlayStation bursts into flames, your character is not dead. You buy another PlayStation, download your save file from the cloud, and your character is exactly where they were, mid-swing.
AI agents are hitting the same inflection point.
Most people think an agent is the model, the runtime, or the loop currently executing the task. Those things matter. But they aren't the agent.
In this piece I'll argue that an agent is its data: specifically its history of events, which we'll call the log. When the log is constructed correctly, an agent can be resumed from it alone. And that single property unlocks a whole set of capabilities that make even advanced agent use cases easier to reason about and build into everyday applications.
##
Defining the agent
So what is the log? Defining the agent means defining the log. At its core, the log is the event history: every user input, model output, tool call, and tool result that accumulates as the agent works: an append-only record of everything that happened.
The log also carries a reference to the session definition: the system prompt, tool descriptions, and skills the agent is running under. This doesn't change from turn to turn, so it's more a versioned constant than an active part of the stream.
Together they form the agent’s full state. Nothing the agent is lives in the runtime, the model, or the tools; they're just interpreters and appenders. They read the durable state, act on it, and write the next event back. So you can hand a fresh executor the same log and it will reconstruct exactly where the agent was and continue from there. The log is enough, on its own, to resume the agent.
##
The log in practice
Once you define the agent as the log, the rest of the system gets easier to reason about. Every operation on the agent either reads the log, appends to it, or renders a view of it. The model reads a view and produces the next action. The tool runner executes a tool call and appends the result. The UI reads the log and renders a timeline; the tracing system reads it and renders traces; an auditor reads it to reconstruct what happened. It's the same pattern databases settled on years ago: the tables, indexes, and caches are all projections over an underlying log of changes. (diagram below adapted from
[@dexhorthy](https://x.com/@dexhorthy)
excellent
[12-factor agents](https://github.com/humanlayer/12-factor-agents)
; worth a read if you haven't.)
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKhMheraAAAdYj7?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ishaansehgal/article/2065129901427130678/media/2064984567203889152)
A high-level agent control loop, running on the log.
In practice, a simplified loop can look like this:
> while session\_has\_work: take\_temporary\_lease(session\_id) state = reconstruct\_from\_log(session\_id) response =
>
> [model.next](http://model.next/)
>
> (state) append(response, to=session\_log) if response.requests\_tool: append(tool\_call\_started, to=session\_log) result = run\_tool(response.tool\_call) append(result, to=session\_log) continue finish\_turn(session\_id)

Harness 系列文章之 3，Tools Are Contracts。
如果 Coding Agent 拥有一个世界，那么每次 tool call，就是用 generated text 请求改变其世界的状态。
Tool call 很容易显得过于简单，model 输出 JSON，Harness parse 它，某个本地 function 被执行，result 被放回下一轮 prompt。
这是 tiny agent 版本。
但 coding agent 的 tool call，并非简单的 function。
Tool call 来自 generated text，它正在请求访问 workspace，shell，network，transcript，或者另一个 Agent。
这个差异会改变整个 Coding Agent 的状态和所处的环境。
> The model can ask. The harness decides.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkMgKnXAAADYXo?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/dongxi%5Fnlp/article/2065200644802101633/media/2065195650870870016)
##
The Proposal and Contract
想象 model 输出：
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkMrEdXUAAy4Ba?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/dongxi%5Fnlp/article/2065200644802101633/media/2065195838196895744)
它看起来很 structured，它依然只是一份 proposal。
Model 产出了看似合法的 JSON，并不自动获得 write access。
Harness 仍然需要回答：
* 这个 tool 是否存在？
* args 是否匹配 schema？
* path 是否在 workspace 内？
* 这是 create、overwrite，还是 patch？
* model 最近是否读过现有文件？
* file-state baseline 是否 fresh？
* 这个 action 是否需要 approval？
* approval 前应该给 human 看什么？
* 多少 result output 可以安全进入 context？
* 执行之后需要更新哪些 transcript 和 state？
这一串问题，就是 tool contract。
##
The Naive Design
naive design 会把 tools 当作一个 function map：
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkNL9vXcAAGhxC?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/dongxi%5Fnlp/article/2065200644802101633/media/2065196403329036288)
这段代码很短，所以看起来干净， 但它同时把很多责任压进了一行。
Parsing，schema validation，path safety，permission policy，sandbox choice，execution，output clipping，transcript recording，state updates，全都被塞进 tool(...)
Demo 可以这样写。但能够修改真实 repo 的 coding agent，需要更强的边界。问题不在 function 本身，问题在于 tool boundary 有不同的 trust rules。
Function call vs Tool call
> 普通程序里，function call 是 implementation detail。
> coding agent 里，tool call 是 generated text 请求改变真实世界的位置。
##
What A Tool Contract Contains
有用的 tool contract 不能只有 name 和 handler。它应该描述：
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkNvI8XsAAyVJu?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/dongxi%5Fnlp/article/2065200644802101633/media/2065197007631790080)
有些字段面向 model。有些字段只属于 harness。
Model 需要足够的信息来正确发起请求，Harness 需要足够的 metadata 来正确裁决。
##
The Lifecycle
一个最小可用 lifecycle：
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkOJkQXYAA-uZh?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/dongxi%5Fnlp/article/2065200644802101633/media/2065197461640011776)
每一步拦截不同类型的问题。
* parse 处理 malformed output
* schema validation 处理 missing fields 和 wrong types
* path validation 处理 workspace escape
* policy 处理 risky action、approval、sandbox、denial
* execution 运行真实 handler
* bounding 避免一次 command 或 file read 淹没下一轮 prompt
* recording 让下一轮可以恢复和审计
所以，“just call the function” 这个 mental model 不够用，function 只是 lifecycle 中的很小片段。
##
Validate Before Approval
validation 应该发生在 approval 之前。
* 如果 patch\_file 指向 workspace 外，先 reject
* 如果 old\_text 缺失或有歧义，先 reject
* 如果 tool call 立刻重复上一轮失败请求，先 reject 或 retry
* 如果 write 目标是现有文件，但缺少 fresh baseline，先 reject
* approval 是 product surface
用户不应该被要求判断一个本来就无效的请求。，需要 approval 时，summary 应该保持 bounded。
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKkOol-XQAA-cKL?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/dongxi%5Fnlp/article/2065200644802101633/media/2065197994677321728)
文件编辑的 approval prompt 应该展示 affected path 和 change shape，避免倾倒 unbounded raw content。
Harness 可以之后展示 diff，count，preview。Approval boundary 要小而清楚。
##
Bounded Results Are

99% people are using /goal and loops wrong.
The hype they hear is "long-running loops prompting autonomous agent": point it at a task, walk away, come back to working code.
But top agentic engineers have been doing that without /goal for 6 months (when GPT-5.2 and Opus 4.5 came out). It's called harness engineering + spec-driven development:
1. build a harness for agent to observe the problem
2. write a tight spec with all the test cases
3. let Codex or Claude Code loop unattended until it meets every one.
I kick these off overnight constantly — 2-5 hours a run. In April one chewed through a Turbo build-cache bug across our Vercel monorepo and had it green by morning. No /goal is actually required.

item.content:encoded:
Sidebar (@SidebarIO)

UI Skills for Design Engineers | Curated Skill Directory https://www.ui-skills.com/?ref=sidebar https://t.co/91BD4i7u1h

🔗 UI Skills for Design Engineers | Curated Skill Directory

🔗 The Four Design Jobs AI Created (So Far) - NN/G

What Does “AI Design” Mean?
When someone says “AI design,” everyone in the room pictures something different.
One person is thinking about using AI to generate component variations for a design system. Another is designing a chat interface. A third is structuring data so an AI agent can parse it. A fourth is defining an LLM’s behavior.
They all fall under “AI design” but they are not the same work.
I see this in job postings, LinkedIn posts, and conference talks. Someone says, “We need to figure out our AI design strategy,” and every person at the table nods — while imagining a completely different thing. Six months later, everyone’s frustrated because the “AI-design initiative” was not what they expected.
The conversation around AI and design is forking. What used to be a single (admittedly vague) topic has split into at least four distinct orientations. Each one focuses on a different type of design work, sits in different organizational structures, and uses different definitions of what “good” looks like. Most teams are staffed for only one of these orientations, confused about which one they’re doing, or trying to dance between all of them without realizing it.
So, which of the four AI design orientations are you in?
The Engine and the Car
An AI model is an engine. A powerful, complex piece of technology under the hood. You can buy just the engine (companies like Anthropic and OpenAI sell directly to developers through their APIs). But most people never experience AI that way.
Most people experience AI inside a “car”: the dashboard, the steering wheel, the seatbelt — all the parts that turn raw capability into something a person can actually drive. Most people don’t care how the engine works. They care that it gets them where they’re going.
This metaphor brings us to the four different meanings of “AI design”. Each of these meanings implies a different kinds of work, skills, questions, and success metrics. They’re not mutually exclusive, but they are very different.
The Four Meanings of “AI Design”
[Laura Costantino](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lauracostantino/) sketched an early version of this framework in [a LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/lauracostantino_ai-design-what-i-think-we-can-simplify-share-7437301579491201024-w4S8?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAAaiZ8sBnWYk4RbV4A-hfCGQVp8VWvD9v3s). I've taken it in a different direction by reworking one of the categories and building out the rest.
1. Designing with AI
You’re the driver. You're the driver behind the wheel.
This is the orientation most people think of first. You use AI in your design process: to [ideate](https://www.nngroup.com/topic/ux-ideation/), [prototype](https://www.nngroup.com/topic/prototyping/), generate [copy](https://www.nngroup.com/contents/self-paced-courses/informative-microcopy-titles-headings-cards-and-more/), build [mood boards](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/mood-boards/), run [competitive research/](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/competitive-usability-evaluations/)audits, or [critique](https://www.nngroup.com/contents/self-paced-courses/design-critiques-getting-actionable-feedback/) your own work. AI tools are your vehicles, and you use them to get somewhere further, faster.
This is where most designers live right now, and there’s nothing wrong with that. AI-as-tool is transformative for how design work gets done. Entire workflow steps that used to take hours now happen in minutes.
The pitfall is treating this type of work as all there is to “AI design.” Leadership says “we’re incorporating AI into our design practice” and what they mean is “our designers are using Claude Code now.” While this type of AI design is a start, it ignores every other way AI is reshaping design opportunity inside the organization.
2. Designing AI Products
You’re the manufacturer. You're building the car (or duct-taping AI onto one that's already moving).
This is where you design the product or interface that delivers AI capabili

item.content:encoded:
Zed (@zeddotdev)

Great software always took shape in conversation, not the commit. With agents, the conversation that generates the code is becoming the true source of our software. And Git can't keep up.

So we built something that can. Meet DeltaDB: https://zed.dev/blog/introducing-deltadb

🔗 Software Is Made Between Commits — Zed's Blog

I have never been a big fan of pull requests.
Before agents, it was easier to believe that the ceremony of trading comments on snapshots was an effective way to collaborate on software, but it never really worked for the Zed team. We frequently work together in the same worktree, building trust and shared understanding by discussing the code as we write it. GitHub doesn't let you talk about code until after you commit and push, but by then our most important conversations are usually already over.
So in 2021, we founded Zed to move beyond the constraints of commits. Our plan was to [build an editor worthy of the world's best developers](https://zed.dev/blog/zed-1-0), then offer a better way to work together inside it. We didn't foresee then how the problems we'd spent years thinking about in the context of human-to-human collaboration would become even more important when collaborating with agents.
Increasingly, the conversation that generates the code is becoming the true source of our software. That conversation unfolds continuously and must be cross-referenced to the code as it changes. Git, organized around discrete commits, was never designed to support this.
So we're building something that is. We call it DeltaDB, a new kind of version control built on a single coherent abstraction that transforms your conversations with agents and the worktrees they edit into shared artifacts. We've made a ton of progress [since I first spoke about it last fall](https://zed.dev/blog/sequoia-backs-zed), and with a [beta version](https://zed.dev/deltadb) ready in a few weeks, I'm excited to share more about what we're launching.
[Every operation, not just every commit](https://zed.dev#every-operation-not-just-every-commit)
DeltaDB breaks your work into a stream of fine-grained deltas. Where Git captures a snapshot at each commit, DeltaDB captures every operation in between and gives each one a stable identity. Because every delta can be addressed on its own, you can point to the code at any moment in its evolution, even as it keeps changing. That lets us version a worktree as it evolves, together with the conversation driving it.
A message and the edit it produced are recorded side by side, so neither drifts away from the other. Because DeltaDB embeds conflict-free replicated worktrees, many people and agents can edit the same files at once across different machines. The files are real: agents work in them through a terminal, and you can mount the whole worktree to disk whenever you want your own tools on it.
[Source code is now source conversation](https://zed.dev#source-code-is-now-source-conversation)
Because every reference is anchored to a delta instead of a line number, it survives as the code moves underneath it. From any line in a past conversation, you can jump to that code as it stands now or as it stood the moment the agent wrote it. From any line of code, you can find the conversation that produced it and every conversation that has touched it since.
Agents can draw on it too. They pick up the context behind the code they're touching or convene the prior agents that worked on it and ask why it's written the way it is.
[You shouldn't need to commit to collaborate](https://zed.dev#you-shouldnt-need-to-commit-to-collaborate)
What we're really after is simple: the conversation with the agent becomes the only conversation you need to have. A teammate can join while the work is still happening, talk to the agent that did the work, and annotate as they go, without waiting for you to commit and push first.
Pull requests, review threads, and inline comments exist to reattach a discussion to code after the fact because the discussion and the code lived in separate places. Put them in the same place, and the ceremony disappears. Git and CI stay for what they're good at: running checks and connecting you to the rest of the world, rather than being the place collaboration is forced to happen.
[What comes next](https://zed.dev#what-comes-ne

🔗 DeltaDB — Early Access

Product Resources Extensions Docs Business Pricing P Sign up S Download D Early Access Software is made between commits Be among the first to try DeltaDB, a version control system that records the work as it unfolds and keeps every change connected to the conversation that shaped it. Learn about DeltaDB Email GitHub username Request Early Access We'll only use this to contact you about DeltaDB's early access. Rewind to any edit DeltaDB captures every operation in between commits and gives each one a stable identity, so you can point to the code at any moment in its evolution. Trace code to conversation Every change is linked to the agent conversation that produced it. From any line of code, find the conversation. From any message, jump to the code it touched. Branch at any moment DeltaDB virtualizes the worktree, so spinning up a new agent branch is effectively free. Any point in history is a valid branch point, including mid-run. Share the thread, not the PR A teammate can join while the work is still happening, talk to the agent that did the work, and annotate as they go, without waiting for you to commit and push first. item.content:encoded:
Matt Stockton (@mstockton)

This is obv. making the rounds. A key adjacent idea I find interesting:

There are lots of companies and orgs sitting on data that could be repurposed as extremely valuable ground truth. Maybe to solve their problems better, but maybe as ground truth accelerator for something totally different.

These companies may have no intention to use the data that way, or even an understanding that they can.

For many of these companies, it’s certain that folks are inquiring about that data and how they can buy ot or use it.

But I am guessing for some of them (maybe long tail) they simply don’t know and no one is telling them.

I think about this opportunity constantly - there is so much data sitting around, ready to be unlocked in interesting / unexpected ways by these models.

And lots of it is probably sitting in the most obscure places you can even imagine.

Never been a better time to explore weird areas and just pick up the rocks to see what’s under them

b2b deals stall because of how the human brain handles RISK, especially risk shared across a group.
once you understand the wiring underneath it, the cycle starts looking predictable,
which means it finally looks like something you can move on purpose instead of something that just happens to you and you can't control...
##
the real competitor is doing nothing:
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKd9OUiXwAAkHM1?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/DinScales26/article/2064758924369166403/media/2064756639157174272)
most reps think they're competing against other vendors.
they build battle cards against the three obvious rivals and rehearse why they win the bake off.
BUT, the actual competitor in nearly every b2b deal is the status quo. doing nothing
gartner style research has repeatedly put "no decision" as the outcome in a HUGE share of qualified opportunities, larger than any single competitor's win rate.
you're usually losing to inertia
the reason is loss aversion, one of the most replicated findings in behavioral science.
people feel the pain of a loss roughly twice as hard as the pleasure of an equivalent gain
run that through the buyer's head. switching risks a visible, personal loss if it goes wrong, the kind their boss remembers at review time.
staying put feels safe EVEN WHEN the status quo bleeds them every month, because the cost of doing nothing is invisible and spread out while the cost of a bad yes is sharp and has their name on it...
so your pitch about upside is fighting a brain hardwired to fear the downside twice as loudly.
this is why why hammering harder on features does nothing.
you're basically adding weight to the side of the scale that was already winning lol
while the side that actually controls the decision, perceived risk, sits UNTOUCHED
##
buying is a group decision, and groups freeze:
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKd9TotW0AAb7Wo?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/DinScales26/article/2064758924369166403/media/2064756730471305216)
real b2b purchases run through committees.
six, eight, sometimes a dozen stakeholders, each with their own risk tolerance, their own boss, their own quiet reason to delay
every person you add multiplies the odds that one of them says "let's revisit next quarter." consensus is fragile.
it only takes ONE nervous voice to stall the whole thing
nobody on a buying committee wants to be the person who championed the thing that failed.
the upside of a good call gets shared across the group, but the downside of a bad one lands on whoever pushed it
so the rational individual move is to just hedge and stay quiet.
multiply that across eight people and you get a room full of professionals all silently incentivized not to move
this is why deals that feel done suddenly go quiet. a SINGLE stakeholder got nervous and pulled the brake
a few smaller biases compound it. ambiguity aversion means anything vague in your pitch quietly reads as risk and pushes them toward doing nothing.
anchoring means the first number they hear frames everything after it
and social proof cuts both ways: if a buyer's peers haven't moved, inaction feels validated. but if you show that companies exactly like them already made this exact decision and it worked, you flip that same instinct onto YOUR SIDE
##

most agency owners give linkedin outbound 90 days before they decide it doesn't work. i'm going to argue that's about 75 days too long. a dialled linkedin outbound campaign tells you whether your offer can scale in the first 7 days.
sometimes the first 7 hours.
the reason almost NOBODY knows this is because they've never seen a campaign that was actually dialled. what most agencies sell you under the name "outbound" is a 90-day waiting game.
by month 2 you know it isn't working but you've already paid two retainers and you're stuck paying the third because everyone you've spoken to has told you it takes time.
it DOESN'T take time.
it takes a real list, a proper offer, and a way to read what's happening before you're $24k deep. i'll walk you through exactly what a working campaign tells you in week 1, week 2, and week 4 - and what each silence means.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKirz5sW0AAH2rs?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/DinScales26/article/2065095783678914853/media/2065089337297915904)
#
what the speed of a campaign tells you
a campaign reacts the SAME day it goes live when the underlying offer is right. one of ours did 5 booked calls in 2 hours from a fresh launch.
another did a 44.7% interested rate three hours after the first messages went out.
the morgan stanley vp who replied to one of our enterprise inmails did it in 4 hours.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKitMvdXYAAmjXR?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/DinScales26/article/2065095783678914853/media/2065090863559041024)
the gtm director at userevidence sent his calendly link back within HOURS of getting the message. none of these were the result of "warmup."
we didn't run a sequence. we didn't drip.
one message landed, the person on the other end had the problem we sell to, and the conversation started. across 30 b2b verticals and 100,000+ inmails sent, the campaigns that work signal in days.
the campaigns that don't also signal in days.
the wait is not the diagnostic. the wait is what you do when you've already missed the diagnostic.
##
what week 1 should actually look like
at the volume we run, a campaign is sending about 1,000 cold messages in its first 5-7 days from a single id-verified account.
if your campaign isn't doing volume like that, the timeline numbers below shift - but the principle holds. inside those first 7 days, you should see at least one of these three things:• a positive reply with no booking intent
someone saying "interesting timing, but we're not buying this quarter."
you've found someone with the problem who isn't ready. that's a real signal - your targeting is working.• a referral
someone saying "not me but you should talk to X at our company."
this is the highest-quality possible signal in week 1\.
it means your message landed with someone close enough to a buyer that they could think of one off the top of their head.• a booked call
obvious one. fewer of these in week 1 unless the campaign is unusually hot. if you've sent 1,000 messages and gotten zero of the three across 7 days, your list or your offer is wrong.
not your copy or channel. one of the upstream variables.
we've seen campaigns sit completely flat for a week and then book 23 qualified leads in the next 7 days after changing a single line of the

Tweet: https://x.com/browser_use/status/2064780286454542690 Primary URLs: - https://browser-use.com/posts/fetch-use Linked content: - A Python Program To Scrape Any Website: https://browser-use.com/posts/fetch-use A Python Program To Scrape Any Website Use our Python SDK to scrape any website instantly and without being blocked. item.content:encoded:
Browser Use (@browser_use)

We launched Fetch Use, the easiest way to scrape any website with the stealthiest browser on the planet.

Proxies, cookies, and sessions are all handled for you, so you don't worry about getting blocked.

See our blog post for more:
https://browser-use.com/posts/fetch-use

🔗 A Python Program To Scrape Any Website

A Python Program To Scrape Any Website
Use our Python SDK to scrape any website instantly and without being blocked.
You found a website with data you need. Maybe it is a list of products, or maybe it is an article. You want a simple Python script that opens the page, extracts the data, and gives you something useful.
A normal Python request often gets blocked or redirected, and scraping can be complex. This is exactly what fetch-use is for.
What is fetch-use?
fetch-use is a Python SDK for getting content from websites the way a real browser would.
This matters because the webpage you see is often not the same page your scraper sees. A site might send different HTML, redirect you, or block the request entirely.
With fetch-use, you can provide a URL and get back the page in a format that is easier to work with. It handles all of the annoying parts of web scraping.
If you are still deciding between a simple scraper and a full browser agent, read our [web scraping guide](https://browser-use.com/posts/web-scraping-guide-2026).
How does fetch-use work?
When you call fetch-use, your script sends a request to Browser Use. Browser Use fetches the URL in a way that looks much closer to a real browser than a normal Python script, handles details like redirects, cookies, sessions, and response formatting, and then returns the response to your Python program.
Install fetch-use
Install the SDK:
Set your Browser Use API key:
You can create an API key in [Browser Use Cloud](https://cloud.browser-use.com/settings?tab=api-keys&new=1).
Your first request
Here is the easiest way to get started:
Give fetch-use a URL, and it gives you back the page.
The response object includes the fields you expect:
If you are calling an API endpoint that returns JSON, parse the response body directly:
Use markdown output for readable pages
Raw HTML is usually noisy. A page might include navigation, scripts, styles, footers, tracking tags, layout markup, and other content that has nothing to do with the data you actually want.
For articles, docs, product descriptions, and other text-heavy pages, output_format="markdown" is often easier to work with:
Instead of parsing a large HTML document immediately, you can start with cleaner text.
Use structured output to inspect a page
When you are exploring a page for the first time, you may not know what is available yet. You might want the title, links, headings, forms, or tables before deciding how to scrape it.
Use output_format="structured":
This is useful when you want to understand the shape of a page before writing a more specific scraper.
Keep cookies with a session
Some sites only make sense across multiple requests. The first page sets cookies, the second page expects them, and the third page changes depending on what happened before.
Use a session_id to keep that state:
Requests with the same session_id share the same session, so cookies can carry over from one request to the next.
Send a POST request
You can also use fetch-use for endpoints that expect data:
This is especially useful when a website loads data from an API behind the page.
Handle errors
For real scripts, always check whether the request worked before parsing the result:
Or check the status code directly:
Complete example
Here is a small script that fetches a page and saves the readable version to a file:
And here is the same idea using structured output:
When should you use a browser instead?
fetch-use is best when you want page content without opening a full browser.
Use browser automation when the page requires interaction:
- clicking buttons
- filling out forms
- scrolling to load more data
- completing a login flow
- waiting for JavaScript-rendered content
- handling a browser challenge or CAPTCHA
For many scraping tasks, though, starting with fetch-use is faster and simpler than opening a browser first.
If you do need a real browser, use Browser Use:
Use fetch-use when you just need the page content. Use Browser Use when the site needs click

for years the meta ads library research process looked like this:
open a browser. manually search competitor after competitor. screenshot interesting ads into a messy google doc. try to remember what you were looking for. spend 45 minutes to get 10 minutes of useful intelligence. build your angle strategy from half-remembered observations and gut feel.
that workflow is over.
claude fable 5 is anthropic's new state-of-the-art vision model. and "vision" here goes way past looking at one image and describing it. fable 5 does autonomous visual navigation at a level no previous model could match. it can scroll, browse, screenshot, extract, and analyze at a depth that makes manual research feel like reading by candlelight.
here's exactly how we're using it to find winning ad angles faster than any human researcher could.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKdtJG2W0AEQSf8?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/zackpaid/article/2064739027484287329/media/2064738957397512193)
##
what fable 5's vision capabilities actually mean
the announcement said fable 5 is "state-of-the-art for tasks involving vision" and can "rebuild a web app's source code from screenshots alone."
that second sentence is the one that matters for advertisers.
it means fable 5 reads the architecture behind a landing page or ad creative, not just the surface of it. the structural decisions. the copywriting framework. the psychological triggers embedded in the layout. the conversion mechanics.
previous models needed complex harnesses and scaffolding to navigate visual environments. fable 5 does it with a minimal, vision-only setup.
for competitive research, this means you can now have an autonomous research agent that:
* browses the meta ads library on your behalf
* identifies and categorizes every competitor angle it finds
* analyzes which creatives have been running longest (the surest proxy for what's working)
* extracts specific copy patterns, hook structures, and visual approaches
* cross-references findings against your own account's historical performance
all without you touching a browser.
##
workflow 1: autonomous competitive research with claude cowork
claude cowork is the desktop tool that lets claude operate your computer directly, clicking, scrolling, and extracting information from any application or website.
paired with fable 5's vision capabilities, it becomes an autonomous research analyst.
the setup:
open claude cowork. assign fable 5 as the model. give it this instruction:
"go to the meta ads library at
[facebook.com/ads/library](http://facebook.com/ads/library)
. search for \[COMPETITOR NAMES AND CATEGORY\]. for every ad that has been running for more than 3 months, extract: the ad angle, the hook structure, the visual format, the estimated audience, and the landing page destination. organize findings by angle type and flag the top 5 creatives by estimated longevity. compile into a structured competitive intelligence report."
fable 5 navigates the library, scrolls through results, identifies run dates, clicks through to landing pages, reads copy, and produces a structured report.
what used to take 45 minutes of tedious manual work takes 8 minutes of autonomous research.

Most agency owners do not have a capacity problem. They have a repetition problem.
The same proposal structure. The same onboarding questions. The same follow-up email when a client goes quiet. The same brief summary written three different ways for three different clients. Hours spent on work that keeps the business alive but does not move it forward.
That is the problem. Here is what solving it actually looks like.
The Business
Marcus runs a one-person brand strategy consultancy. He works with three to five clients at a time, charges mid-to-high market rates, and had been stuck at the same revenue ceiling for two years. Not because he lacked clients. Because he kept running out of hours.
His week looked like this: fifteen hours of billable work, twelve hours of admin, proposals, emails, and meeting prep. The math was broken before he even opened his laptop.
Stage One: Audit Before You Automate
The instinct is to jump straight into building prompts. That is the wrong move.
Marcus spent one week logging every task he repeated. Not estimating. Logging. At the end of the week he had a list of twenty-three recurring tasks. Fourteen of them were language-based. Proposals, briefs, status updates, scope clarification emails, LinkedIn posts from workshop notes, onboarding documents.
He did not need a new tool. He needed those fourteen tasks systematized.
The prompt he used for this audit:
> "I run a solo brand strategy consultancy. Here is my typical week: \[pasted log\]. Identify which tasks are language-based and could be handled or accelerated with an AI writing system. Group them by frequency and time cost."
Claude returned a prioritized list in under two minutes. The top three were proposals, client onboarding briefs, and project status summaries. Combined, they were eating nine hours a week.
Stage Two: Build the System, Not the Shortcut
This is where most business owners get it wrong.
They ask Claude to write one proposal. It comes out decent. They feel good. Then next week they start from scratch again and wonder why results vary. That is not automation. That is assisted typing.
Marcus built a Claude Project for each core workflow.
For proposals, the project system prompt included his positioning, his pricing logic, his typical client objections, and three anonymized past proposals as style references. The project remembered context across every session. It did not need re-explaining. It did not forget his tone between uses.
His proposal prompt:
> "Client: \[name and company\]. Industry: \[sector\]. Problem they described: \[paste discovery call notes\]. Budget signal: \[high/medium/unclear\]. Write a proposal using my standard structure. Keep the tone direct. Flag any section where you need more information before I send this."
First draft in four minutes. Editing time down from ninety minutes to twenty. The output was not perfect. It never is. But it was eighty percent of the way there, and editing a draft is fundamentally faster than generating one from nothing.
For onboarding, he built a second project. System prompt included his full onboarding process, the questions he asks every new client, his communication style, and a note about what tends to confuse new clients in the first two weeks. New client int

#
The $1,718 per 2 weeks
Last 2 weeks X paid me $1,718 in revenue sharing. Not for selling a course. Not for ads. For doing the thing I'd already be doing anyway - digging through AI tools all day and posting what I find.
Here's the part nobody sees: the routine behind this account isn't done by me anymore. It’s handled by an agent I use on a daily basis. It reads the feed, scores topics, learns from my analytics and writes drafts in my voice. I just pick, tweak and hit publish.
This article is the exact system. Not theory - the actual files, the actual code, the actual numbers.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKe8lAGW4AAmVos?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/seelffff/article/2064831856164430010/media/2064826298040508416)
#
How It Works
One run, four stages. No frameworks, no orchestration - a script, a model, and three markdown files.
1. Collect. The script pulls GitHub trending, the Hacker News front page, and my inbox file - a note where I dump anything that caught my eye during the day: links, questions from my replies, half-formed ideas.
2. Score. The model gets all of it together with my style, my memory and my analytics - and ranks the 5 best topics. Each topic gets a score out of 10, a format, and one line on why my audience would care.
3. Draft. For the top 2 topics it writes complete posts in my voice, in both languages, plus an idea for the visual - what to record or screenshot.
4. Review. I read, kill what's weak, tweak what's good, publish. The agent never posts anything itself. That's not a technical limitation - that's the design.
![](https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2064824561019850752/img/PvlI1wA2qkSycaiO.jpg)
After every run the agent saves a note like this into topics/ - a real example, trimmed to three topics:
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKeicfMWYAASvbZ?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/seelffff/article/2064831856164430010/media/2064797564465995776)
How to read it: topic - score out of 10 - which of my 7 formats fits. The line below is the argument - why my audience specifically would care. The score comes from four factors: how fresh the topic is, whether there are concrete numbers to hook with, how it matches my audience's interests from analytics, and whether big accounts have already covered it. That's exactly why topic #3 got a 6/10 - solid story, but the window had closed.
#
The Folder
Everything lives in one folder inside my Obsidian vault. Plain markdown plus one Python script. If I delete the script tomorrow, the brain survives - it's all in the files.
plaintext
```plaintext
agent/
├── style.md - how I write (the agent's taste)
├── memory.md - what's been posted, what's rejected
├── analytics.md - what actually works, from real numbers
├── replies.md - how I comment on other people's posts
├── agent.py - the agent itself (~100 lines)
├── topics/
│ ├── inbox.md - raw material I collect during the day
│ └── scored topics land here after every run
└── drafts/
└── ready-to-post drafts land here
```
#
Brain #1: style.md - the Agent's Taste
The agent doesn't “write like an AI” because it's not allowed to. I exported 182 of my posts, had the model extract the patterns, then added my own bans on top. The result is a contract the agent can't break:
* everything lowercase, no hashtags, emojis only in memes
* first line is

##
why i'm getting more serious about memory plugins for agents
i run hermes agents on my own server.
when i open a new session, my content agent already knows my voice rules, my red lines, what i rejected last week, and what i'm building toward.
that is the part that still feels wild to me. the agent does not start from zero every time i open the terminal.
it remembers enough to keep working.
i've been digging into agent memory systems because i think this is one of the more important layers people are going to care about soon.
the useful version is simple:
> my agent can carry context across real work without making me re-explain the same project every morning.
some quick context:
i'm not married to one memory layer.
i like testing new agent tools early, especially when they touch the parts that actually matter: cost trust recall boundaries ...and whether the thing still works after the demo.
##
every memory system is basically trying to do the same thing
the simple version:
1. something happens in a session
2. the memory layer decides what is worth keeping
3. it saves that context somewhere
4. later, your agent asks for the useful stuff back
5. the useful stuff gets pulled into the next session
6. you need some way to correct it when it gets weird
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKfNHc8WgAAFgrI?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/cobi%5Fbean/article/2064848575708922093/media/2064844482084765696)
the basic loop behind agent memory
the interesting part is what each system thinks a memory should be.
is it a saved fact?
a searchable note?
a summary?
a model of a person?
a model of a project?
that choice changes everything.
##
the cool part: memory can follow the work
this is the part i care about most.
a good memory layer should not be trapped inside one app. if i'm using multiple agentic tools, i want the context to travel with the work.
right now i have Honcho in a few of my hermes agents. i also have it wired into one project inside codex.
so when i'm building an app or tool, the project does not feel completely cold every time i come back.
it can remember the design direction, the weird bug i already chased, the constraints i keep repeating, and the decisions i do not want to relitigate.
that's the category i care about: portable working memory for agents.
what i'm hunting for is memory that can follow a project across sessions and tools.
##
mem0 feels like a memory database for agents
mem0 is one version of this idea.

IN THE DASHBOARD.

no CLI. no config editing. no guesswork. @NousResearch

MCPs

→ confirm and deploy

What Is Loop Engineering? (And Why It's the Future of AI)
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1983099742784532480/ri6WHAQH_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/dashboardlim)
[Lian Lim | Dashboard & AI Automation Expert](http://x.com/dashboardlim)

1
24
94
[7K](http://x.com/dashboardlim/status/2064736540757012991/analytics)
Loop engineering is designing automated systems that prompt your AI agents instead of you prompting them directly.
You build a small system that finds work, hands it to agents, checks the output, records what's done, and decides what's next.
Then you let that system run while you sleep.
The old way: you type a prompt, read the response, type the next prompt.
The new way: you design the loop once and the loop does the prompting for you.
A few days ago, Boris Cherny said something that made this click for a lot of people.
Cherny is the head of Claude Code at Anthropic.
The guy who built the coding agent that now writes 4% of all GitHub commits.
Here's what he said:
"I don't prompt Claude anymore. I have loops running that prompt Claude and figuring out what to do. My job is to write loops."
That statement went viral.
700,000 views in 24 hours.
Because it named something people were already sensing but couldn't articulate.
The leverage point has moved.
Prompt engineering was the skill of 2024.
Loop engineering is the skill of 2026.
#
The Progression
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKdpRZHWwAAkOcJ?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/dashboardlim/article/2064736540757012991/media/2064734701693091840)
Three years ago, the skill was typing fast.
Two years ago, the skill was prompting well.
One year ago, the skill was running multiple agents in parallel.
Now?
The skill is designing the loop that does all of that without you.
The unit of work moved from the keystroke, to the prompt, to the loop.
Most people are still on step two.
The people building the future are already on step four.
#
The Five Building Blocks
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKdo2WCWQAAIkh4?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/dashboardlim/article/2064736540757012991/media/2064734237010313216)
Every loop needs five things and a place to remember stuff.
Here's the framework.
##
Automations
The heartbeat of the loop.
Scheduled tasks that run on their own.
Discovery and triage without you.
The loop wakes up, finds work, and acts on it while you sleep.
An automation can run every morning, scan your issue tracker, summarize failures, surface what needs attention, and write the findings to a state file.
You wake up to a prioritized list, not an inbox you have to manually process.
##
Worktrees
Isolation so parallel agents don't collide.
Two agents writing the same file is chaos.
Worktrees give each agent its own branch, its own working directory, sharing the same history.
One agent's work cannot touch another's.
This is what makes parallelism possible without everything breaking.
##
Skills
Project knowledge that survives across runs.
Without skills, every loop run is day one.
The agent forgets everything between sessions.
Skills hold the institutional knowledge.
The conventions, the build steps, the context that would otherwise get lost.
Written once, read every run.
##
Connectors
The loop needs to touch your real tools.
Open PRs, update tickets, post to Slack, query databases, trigger actions.
A loop that can only read files is a loop that can only suggest.
A loop with connectors is a loop that operates.
##
Sub-agents
The agent that wrote the output is a poor judge of its own work.
One agent explores

Fable 5 is one day old. I ran
[/last30days](https://github.com/mvanhorn/last30days-skill/)
on it five times, 865 items across Reddit, X, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Hacker News, and Polymarket, while running the model myself the whole time. Here's what survived day one: the best practices, with receipts, and the funniest things the internet said.
##
1\. Give It a Harder Job Than You Think You Should
The official playbook is two words: aim higher. Hand Fable 5 tasks harder than what you gave prior models, let it interview you before executing, and strip the over-prescriptive scaffolding out of your old prompts, because the numbered babysitting steps now degrade output. I tested this on day one and it's real. State the outcome, get out of the way. And never ask it to echo its internal reasoning, which trips refusals per the official guide.
Which makes the funniest comment of the launch even better. On
[Alex Finn's](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RwsUnvHYmyw)
"I'm speechless" video (115K views in a day),
[151 likes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RwsUnvHYmyw)
:
> Buddy said it's a mythos level model then proceeded to create a todo app and a snake game like a good boy
> \- mousepaddd, YouTube
Everyone got told to aim higher. Everyone made a snake game.
##
2\. Set Goals, Not Steps
The biggest workflow change in the corpus: stop walking the model through tasks and start stating destinations.
[Anthropic's own Claude Code team](https://di.gg/ai/zrppa6ui)
says Fable 5 moved their work "from micro-managing tasks to high-level goal alignment," with a new /goal command for continuous operation.
One catch, per
[Simon Willison's](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jun/9/claude-fable-5/)
"slow, expensive and capable" review: it often keeps working until stopped. Write a hard stop rule into every long run, a budget cap, a time cap, or a done condition.
The community immediately found the logical endpoint:
> /goal make 1 million dollars, make no mistake
> \- FreqtradeFR, YouTube,
>
> [92 likes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RwsUnvHYmyw)
##
3\. Run It as an Orchestrator, Not a Worker
Everyone landed on the same architecture within 24 hours.
[@Steve8708](https://x.com/@Steve8708)
's
[verdict](https://x.com/Steve8708/status/2064847457977319735)
: Fable is "a step smarter than GPT 5.5 and Opus" and "needs less babysitting than any other model out there," but "slow and expensive as hell - best used as an orchestrator of cheaper models."
[@aplomb2](https://x.com/@aplomb2)
's routing:
[Fable plans, Sonnet implements, Haiku tests](https://x.com/aplomb2/status/2064838222014984228)
. Half your agents build, half verify, and the verify pass gates the commit.
The launch receipt is absurd on its own: Stripe pointed Fable 5 at a 50-million-line Ruby codebase and shipped a one-day migration a full team had scoped at two months, per
[Anthropic's own announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-fable-5-mythos-5)
.
And the
[definitive write-up](https://x.com/amirmxt/status/2064852788799062308)
of what happens if you skip the routing advice:
> "mom how did we get so poor?" "your dad ran claude fable 5 subagent workflows with no spend limit"
> \-
>
> [@amirmxt](https://x.com/@amirmxt)
##
4\. Work the Effort Dial, Medium Is the Sleeper
Effort

nobody really teaches you research. you get a desk, a problem someone else picked, and a vague instruction to produce something novel. so most people reverse-engineer the job from what they can see, which is papers, threads, and announcements, and what they end up learning is how to look like a researcher rather than how to be one. the actual skill is a stack of smaller skills, and almost every one of them can be deliberately trained.
##
pick your own problems
richard hamming had a habit at bell labs that made him unpopular at lunch. he'd ask whoever sat near him what the important problems in their field were, then ask why they weren't working on them. people changed tables. the question stings because most of us have no good answer. we don't choose problems, we absorb them, from an advisor, from whatever a big lab announced last quarter, from the paper everyone is quote-tweeting this week.
the trouble with an absorbed problem is that you hold the conclusion without the reasoning. you know some famous lab cares about a direction, but not why, not what they expect to find, not what would make them drop it. when they pivot, you find out a year later. and on a problem that's already fashionable, you're racing a thousand people who started earlier and have more compute than you.
john schulman's guide to ml research splits the work into two modes. in one, you read the literature and hunt for things to improve. in the other, you choose an outcome you genuinely want to exist and reason backwards to the experiments. he argues for the second, and the quiet reason is that it manufactures originality. a goal you actually care about will drag you into territory no survey paper covers.
taste, meanwhile, gets discussed like a gift. it behaves more like a muscle. predict the result of every experiment before you run it. cover a paper's results section and guess the numbers from the method alone. mark down which of this month's releases will matter in two years and check your hit rate later. a forecast plus a correction, repeated a few hundred times, is how every good model gets trained, including the one in your head.
##
upgrade your inputs
shared reading lists produce shared ideas. if your information diet is the trending page of arxiv plus whatever survives the group chat filter, you will reliably reach the same conclusions as everyone else, at the same time, which makes those conclusions worth approximately nothing.
old material is criminally underpriced. this field reruns its own past on a delay: mixture of experts dates to 1991, lstms to 1997, backprop went mainstream in 1986\. rich sutton needed about a thousand words in 2019 to write the bitter lesson, and it predicts the shape of the field better than surveys ten times its length. claude shannon gave a talk on creative thinking in 1952 where his opening move was to shrink a problem until it's nearly trivial, crack the small version, then reintroduce the difficulty one piece at a time. that single trick will carry you through more walls than any modern productivity advice.
range matters as much as depth. interpretability borrows shamelessly from neuroscience. eval design is mechanism design wearing a lab coat. a working sense of how gpus actually move memory tells you which architecture papers are doomed before the benchmarks do. and ho

item.content:encoded:
Xiaoyin Qu (@quxiaoyin)

你做了一款好产品。然后呢？

IndieHackers 数据：73% 独立创始人的第一痛点是客户获取，不是产品开发。

我拆解了 2026 年 solo founder 如何用 AI Agent 搭建增长引擎——内容、冷启动、激活、反馈四个引擎的完整路径。

一人公司也能跑增长飞轮 👇

https://tycoon.us/blog/ai-growth-engine-for-indie-founders

🔗 独立创始人最缺的不是产品，是客户：2026 年如何用 AI Agent 做增长

AI 增长引擎和传统营销工具有什么区别？
传统营销工具是「你操作，它执行」——你写邮件，它帮你发。AI 增长引擎是「你设定目标，它自主执行」——你告诉它「本周需要在 Reddit 获取 50 个注册」，它会自己选题、写帖、监控效果、调整策略。区别是自主性和协作能力。
产品只是入场券，增长才是比赛本身——AI Agent 让一人公司也能跑增长飞轮。
产品做好了，客户在哪？这是 2026 年每个独立创始人都在问的问题。本文用真实案例拆解如何用 AI Agent 搭建增长引擎——从冷启动到规模化获客，零营销团队的独立创始人也能做到。
Free to startNo credit card requiredUpdated Jun 2026
IndieHackers 上有一个帖子正在被疯狂讨论——「Building a complex SaaS was the easy part. Now I need proof.」发帖人花了七个月打磨产品，功能齐全、架构干净、性能优秀。然后他停在了一个问题上：谁来用？
这不是个例。500k.io 的 2026 年独立创始人统计数据显示：73% 的独立创始人把「客户获取」列为第一痛点，远超「产品开发」（11%）和「融资」（9%）。
产品做得再好，没人用就是零。
但独立创始人的困境在于：你既没有预算雇增长团队，也没有时间同时搞定产品和营销。结果就是——产品上线了，然后呢？
你在 Product Hunt 上线了，发了 X，发了 Reddit，贴了 HN。24 小时后：12 个 upvote，3 条评论，0 个注册。你的帖子沉了。
不是产品不好——是冷启动本身就是一场信息战争，而一个人打不赢。
你开始写博客、发推、做 LinkedIn。三个月后：博客月访问 200，X 粉丝 300。你发现内容的投入产出比低得可怕——不是因为内容没用，是因为你没有精力同时做内容和分发。
一个博文写 4 小时，分发到 10 个渠道又要 3 小时。一周一篇博文，你每周 7 小时砸在内容上——这还不算选题和数据分析的时间。
Bazzly 的创始人 Filippo 在 IndieHackers 上写了一篇爆文：「You don't need more traffic. You need better activation.」43 个 upvote，70 条评论。核心观点：大多数独立创始人花 80% 时间在「做」增长（发帖、回帖、写邮件），只花 20% 时间在「想」增长（用户洞察、渠道策略、转化优化）。
理想的比例应该反过来。
2026 年的 AI Agent 已经不是「写文案的工具」了。它们能做的是一个完整增长团队的日常工作——从内容生产到多渠道分发，从冷启动 outreach 到客户反馈分析。
一个独立创始人的增长系统只需要四个 AI 角色：
1. AI 内容引擎 → 把「写东西」变成流水线
不是让 AI 替你写一篇文章。是让 AI 跑一整个内容流水线：
- 选题：扫描 IndieHackers、X、Reddit、HN 的热点话题，匹配你的产品定位
- 撰写：基于 SEO 关键词和用户搜索意图生成结构化内容
- 分发：自动生成 X thread、Reddit 帖子、HN 提交文案、Slack/Discord 社区分享
- 追踪：48 小时后复盘数据，标记高转化渠道
一个独立创始人手动跑完这个流程需要 6-10 小时。AI Agent 可以降到 1 小时以内——你的角色从「执行者」变成了「审核者」。
2. AI 冷启动引擎 → 不是 spam，是规模化的人际接触
冷启动最难的是什么？不是找不到目标用户——是一个个联系太慢了。
AI 冷启动引擎的工作流程：
- 识别你的目标用户活跃的社区（Reddit 子版块、Slack 群组、Discord 服务器）
- 监控相关讨论话题
- 生成个性化、有价值的回复（不是「试试我的产品」，而是真正回答问题，自然带出你的产品作为解决方案）
- 跟踪哪些社区和话题的转化率最高
LiFast 的创始人做了一个 AI LinkedIn outreach 工具，自己先用它做冷启动——从 600 次 LinkedIn 资料浏览到 12 个真实客户，只用了 90 天。
3. AI 激活引擎 → 让注册用户真正用起来
大多数独立创始人的激活流程是这样的：用户注册 → 收到一封 welcome email → 然后就没有然后了。
IndieHackers 的数据：一个新用户在注册后 72 小时内如果没有完成「关键动作」（比如完成第一个任务、导入数据、邀请队友），流失率超过 80%。
AI 激活引擎能做什么：
- 根据用户注册时的行为数据，发个性化的 onboarding 序列
- 监控用户的关键行为（登录频率、功能使用、停留时间）
- 在用户即将流失时触发挽留动作（个性化的邮件、教程视频、甚至是一个真实的 demo offer）
这不是「发邮件」——这是用数据驱动的自动化激活。
4. AI 反馈引擎 → 让客户告诉你下一步做什么
增长不等于获客。增长的真正引擎是 客户洞察 → 产品迭代 → 口碑传播。
AI 反馈引擎的工作：
- 自动收集和分析客服对话、社交媒体评论、产品内反馈
- 提取高频需求和痛点
- 标记流失信号（某个功能的使用率突然下降、负面评价集中出现）
- 每周生成一份「你该知道的 5 件事」
你不再是盲飞。
假设你是一个独立创始人，刚上线了一个 AI 项目协作工具。你的增长飞轮怎么跑：
第 1-2 周：内容播种
- AI 内容引擎产出 2 篇 SEO 博文 + 10 条社交分发
- 目标：建立初始内容资产，开始获取搜索流量
第 3-4 周：社区冷启动
- AI 冷启动引擎在 3 个目标社区持续互动
- 每天 5-10 条有价值的回复，自然带出产品
- 目标：获得第一批 20-30 个注册用户
第 5-8 周：激活和迭代
- AI 激活引擎接手新用户 onboarding
- AI 反馈引擎收集用户行为数据和反馈
- 根据数据迭代产品
第 9 周起：规模化
- 内容引擎进入周更节奏
- 冷启动引擎扩展到新社区
- 激活和反馈引擎持续优化
这不是理论——500k.io 的数据显示，使用 AI Agent 做增长的独立创始人，6 个月内用户增长速度是仅靠手动增长的 3.4 倍。
AI 不是魔法。如果你自己的增长策略是错的，AI 只是帮你更快地执行错误策略。
先想清楚：你的目标用户是谁？他们在哪里？他们为什么应该用你的产品？这些问题的答案不能交给 AI。
AI 可以 10 分钟产出一篇博文——但 10 篇平庸的文章不如 1 篇真正有用的文章。AI 内容引擎的起点应该是用户搜索意图研究和竞品内容分析，而不是「让 AI 随便写」。
一个独立创始人的 AI 增长团队应该聚焦在 1-2 个渠道上做到极致，而不是 10 个渠道都蜻蜓点水。
怎么选渠道？看两个指标：
- 你的目标用户在不在这个渠道
- 这个渠道是否适合长期积累（SEO 和社区 > 一次性广告）
如果你只有 1-2 个 AI 工具（ChatGPT 写文案、一个 SEO 工具做关键词），你只是把单项任务自动化了。
真正的增长引擎是 AI Agent 之间的协作：你的 AI 内容引擎自动把博文发给 AI 分发引擎，AI 分发引擎把用户反馈喂给 AI 分析引擎，AI 分析引擎把洞察推给你。
这就是 Tycoon 在解决的问题——不是给你一个 AI 工具，而是给你一个 AI 增长团队：
- [AI CEO](https://tycoon.us/blog/what-is-an-ai-ceo)— 每天早上的优先级清单，自动跟进和堵点发现
- [AI 写手 + SEO + 分发](https://tycoon.us/blog/your-first-employee-should-be-ai)— 内容从选题到多平台分发全自动
- [AI 增长分析师](https://tycoon.us/blog/how-to-run-a-one-person-company-with-ai)— 数据找人，而不是人找数据
你不再是一个人在战斗。
产品做好了，客户在哪？这个问题不会再让你失眠。
FAQ
Clear answers about wallet credit, usage, subscriptions, and how Tycoon charges for work.
传统营销工具是「你操作，它执行」——你写邮件，它帮你发。AI 增长引擎是「你设定目标，它自主执行」——你告诉它「本周需要在 Reddit 获取 50 个注册」，它会自己选题、写帖、监控效果、调整策略。区别是自主性和协作能力。
一个集成 AI 平台的月费通常在 $9-$99 之间，覆盖内容、分发、分析和冷启动。相比之下，雇一个兼职增长人员的成本是 $2K-$5K/月。AI 增长引擎的成本是人类的 1-3%。
Google 的立场很明确：惩罚的是「低质量、为操纵排名而生的内容」，不是「AI 辅助创作的内容」。关键策略是：AI 出草稿和结构，人类把控洞察和真实经验，确保每篇内容提供独特的价值。纯 AI 生成、零人工审核的内容确实有风险。
取决于你的产品类型和目标用户。B2B SaaS 优先 SEO + LinkedIn + 行业社区；B2C 优先 SEO + Reddit + X；开发者工具优先 SEO + HN + GitHub + Dev.to。无论选哪个渠道，聚焦 1-2 个做到 80 分，再考虑扩展。
取决于你怎么用。AI 的正确用法
